name: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture
summary: A partial or complete tear of the ACL, usually from a non-contact deceleration, landing or cutting movement with the knee near extension and collapsing into valgus.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: 9–12 months after reconstruction; rehab-first pathway 3–6 months to stable function

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Not before 9 months post-reconstruction and only once criteria are met

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI confirms and identifies associated meniscal, chondral and bone injuries

overview:
The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) is the primary restraint to anterior translation of the tibia on the femur and a secondary restraint to internal rotation and valgus. Rupture is one of the most consequential injuries in pivoting sports: it causes immediate instability, a haemarthrosis and profound quadriceps inhibition, and it significantly increases the long-term risk of knee osteoarthritis [r1,r19].

Most ruptures are non-contact, occurring within milliseconds of foot strike as an athlete decelerates, lands or changes direction with the knee close to extension [r2,r3]. Management is either rehabilitation first (with reconstruction only if instability persists) or reconstruction plus rehabilitation; in young active adults the two pathways produce similar patient-reported outcomes at two years [r10,r11]. Whichever pathway is chosen, the physiotherapist leads a long, criteria-based rehabilitation that determines function, return to sport (RTS) and re-injury risk [r12,r14].

epidemiology.text: A meta-analysis of 58 studies found that 1 in 29 female athletes (3.5%) and 1 in 50 male athletes (2.0%) sustained an ACL injury over follow-up periods from one season to 25 years; the incidence rate in female athletes was about 1.7 times that of males (1.5 vs 0.9 per 10,000 athlete-exposures) [r1]. Roughly 70% of ruptures occur without contact with another player [r2]. Rupture is most common between 15 and 25 years of age, in sports requiring deceleration, landing and cutting.

intrinsic: Female sex (higher incidence rate, influenced by neuromuscular, anatomical and hormonal factors) [r1]
Dynamic knee valgus and high knee abduction moment on landing (modifiable) [r4]
Previous ACL injury or reconstruction, on either knee [r18]
Young age (<25 years) at return to high-level sport [r18]
Narrow intercondylar notch and increased posterior tibial slope
Generalised joint hypermobility and above-average hamstring flexibility [r2]
extrinsic: Pivoting, cutting and jumping sports (soccer, basketball, netball, handball, football codes)
High shoe–surface friction (e.g. studs on dry artificial turf)
Competition (versus training) and fatigue late in matches
Absence of a neuromuscular injury-prevention program [r20]

mechanism.summary: The classic non-contact ACL rupture happens about 40 ms after initial foot contact during a deceleration, side-step cut or one-leg landing. The knee is only slightly flexed (≈20–30°) and collapses into valgus coupled with internal tibial rotation while ground-reaction forces peak at about three times body weight [r3]. A strong quadriceps contraction near extension adds anterior tibial shear, which the ACL must resist [r2].
sequence: The athlete decelerates sharply to land or change direction, planting the foot flat or heel-first ahead of the body.
At initial contact the knee is near extension (≈20–30° flexion) and the trunk is upright or leaning over the stance leg.
Within ~40 ms the knee collapses into valgus (≈12°) as the hip adducts and internally rotates — 'knee-in, toe-out' [r3,r5].
The tibia rotates internally and is sheared forward by quadriceps pull and ground-reaction force (≈3 × body weight) [r3].
The ACL is loaded beyond its failure strength and ruptures, usually in mid-substance or near its femoral attachment.
The tibia subluxes anteriorly; the lateral femoral condyle impacts the posterolateral tibial plateau (bone bruise), then the tibia rotates externally as the knee reduces.
The athlete feels a 'pop', the knee gives way, and a haemarthrosis develops over the next few hours.

variants.name: Contact (valgus blow)
variants.description: A direct blow to the lateral knee drives it into valgus. This often produces the combined ACL + MCL + meniscal injury.

variants.name: Hyperextension
variants.description: Forced knee hyperextension (e.g. kicking air, awkward landing) can rupture the ACL and may be associated with a PCL or posterolateral corner injury.

variants.name: Skiing 'phantom foot'
variants.description: The skier falls backward with hips below knees, and the tail of the ski acts as a lever that drives the tibia into internal rotation.

variants.name: Boot-induced anterior drawer
variants.description: When landing a jump off balance, the rigid ski boot pushes the tibia forward.

anatomy.text: The ACL runs from the posteromedial aspect of the lateral femoral condyle (inside the intercondylar notch) anteriorly and medially to the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia. It is intra-articular but extra-synovial, has a limited blood supply from the middle genicular artery, and is rich in mechanoreceptors that contribute to knee proprioception. It has two functional bundles. The anteromedial bundle is tight in flexion and the posterolateral bundle is tight near extension.

structures.name: Anterior cruciate ligament
structures.role: Primary restraint to anterior tibial translation (~85% of resistance); secondary restraint to internal rotation and valgus; proprioceptive organ

structures.name: Menisci
structures.role: Load distribution and secondary anterior stability. The posterior horn of the medial meniscus becomes a key restraint in the ACL-deficient knee.

structures.name: Medial collateral ligament
structures.role: Primary restraint to valgus; often injured together with the ACL

structures.name: Quadriceps
structures.role: Extends the knee. Near extension it pulls the tibia forward, which loads the ACL.

structures.name: Hamstrings
structures.role: Flex the knee and pull the tibia backward. They act as the ACL's dynamic agonist.

structures.name: Hip abductors and external rotators
structures.role: Control femoral adduction and internal rotation, the proximal driver of dynamic valgus

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
Ligament collagen is loaded through a toe region (crimp straightening), a linear elastic region and then sequential fibril failure. In a rupture, the combined valgus, internal-rotation and anterior-shear load exceeds the ACL's capacity within milliseconds. Fibres fail at multiple levels, which leaves a 'mop-end' tear, usually in mid-substance or near the femoral footprint. The two stumps retract.

Unlike extra-articular ligaments, the ruptured ACL does not bridge the gap. Synovial fluid dilutes the fibrin clot. Within weeks a synovial lining covers each stump, and myofibroblast-like cells within it may contribute to retraction [r6]. The result is persistent mechanical laxity. In about half of cases the subluxation event also bruises the subchondral bone of the lateral compartment, and it may tear a meniscus or damage articular cartilage, which starts the biological processes that lead to post-traumatic osteoarthritis [r19].

structures.name: ACL
structures.effect: Partial (rare) or complete rupture; stumps retract and do not heal across the gap [r6]

structures.name: Lateral femoral condyle & posterolateral tibial plateau
structures.effect: Impaction 'kissing' bone bruise from anterior tibial subluxation; marker of the pivot event on MRI

structures.name: Menisci
structures.effect: Concomitant tears are common. Lateral tears occur more often acutely. Medial (posterior horn) tears accumulate with recurrent giving way.

structures.name: Medial collateral ligament
structures.effect: Sprain in valgus-contact and combined mechanisms

structures.name: Articular cartilage
structures.effect: Chondral contusion and matrix damage at impact, an early step toward post-traumatic osteoarthritis [r19]

structures.name: Anterolateral capsule / ligament complex
structures.effect: May be injured with high-grade rotatory instability (large pivot shift)

muscles.name: Quadriceps
muscles.effect: Arthrogenic muscle inhibition (AMI). Effusion, inflammation and loss of ligament afferents reduce voluntary activation. The result is lag, rapid atrophy and persistent weakness that can last years [r7].

muscles.name: Hamstrings
muscles.effect: Protective co-activation increases. They become the main dynamic restraint to anterior tibial translation in the ACL-deficient knee.

muscles.name: Gluteals and calf
muscles.effect: Altered recruitment and disuse weakness. Proximal (hip) control deficits persist and contribute to re-injury risk.

cellular.description: Torn vessels bleed into the joint, and platelets release growth factors and cytokines. Neutrophils and then macrophages infiltrate the ligament remnants [r6].
A synovial layer containing α-smooth-muscle-actin cells forms over the stumps (resynovialisation) instead of a bridging scar [r6].
Cell density and blood vessels increase within the remnants, but tissue never bridges the femoral and tibial ends [r6].

The remnants remodel or are resorbed. After reconstruction, the tendon graft undergoes necrosis, revascularisation and remodelling toward a ligament-like tissue ('ligamentisation'). The timeframe of this process in humans is uncertain [r13].

systems.effect: Loss of ACL mechanoreceptor input and joint effusion alter spinal reflex excitability (AMI) [r7]. Chronic ACL deficiency changes brain activation patterns in sensorimotor areas. This supports treating ACL injury as a neurophysiological dysfunction as well as a mechanical one [r8].
Haemarthrosis and synovitis raise intra-articular cytokines and degradative enzymes. These stress chondrocytes and initiate post-traumatic osteoarthritis pathways [r19].
Gait and landing adapt to avoid quadriceps load. Movement shifts toward the hip and ankle and to the uninjured limb. Limb-symmetry deficits persist long after pain resolves.
Fear of re-injury, reduced confidence and threatened athletic identity are common. They predict failure to return to the pre-injury level of sport [r16,r17].
About 50% of people develop radiographic knee osteoarthritis 10–20 years after an ACL or meniscal injury, whether or not they have surgery [r19].

grading.system: Anatomical sprain grade (with instrumented / clinical laxity)

grades.description: Microscopic fibre damage; no increase in anterior laxity; firm Lachman end-feel.
Some fibres torn, sometimes one bundle. Laxity is increased but the end-feel stays firm. Partial tears may progress to complete with further instability.
grades.prognosis: Often managed conservatively; monitor for functional instability

grades.description: Complete loss of continuity. Laxity is increased with a soft or absent Lachman end-feel, and the pivot shift is positive.
grades.prognosis: Rehab-first or reconstruction pathway depending on instability, sport and patient goals

timeframes.summary: The native ACL does not heal across the gap. Recovery reflects resolution of effusion and AMI, restoration of strength and neuromuscular control, and (after reconstruction) graft incorporation. Time is necessary but never sufficient for progression.

healing.description: Bleeding, effusion and inflammatory cell infiltrate; quadriceps inhibition is greatest
Synovial covering forms over the stumps; no bridging
Neovascularisation and increased cellularity of remnants (or early graft revascularisation after reconstruction)
Remnant or graft remodelling; graft maturation continues beyond 12 months

milestones.label: Full extension, quiet knee
milestones.note: Priority in the first 2 weeks after injury or surgery

milestones.label: Start running
milestones.note: Once criteria are met (e.g. no effusion, ~70–80% quadriceps symmetry)

timeframes.returnToSport: 9–12+ months after reconstruction; it is criteria-based rather than time-based. Re-injury risk falls by about 51% for each month RTS is delayed up to 9 months [r14].

symptoms: Felt or heard a 'pop' at the moment of injury
Immediate pain and inability to continue playing
Episodes of the knee 'giving way' during pivoting once acute pain settles
Difficulty fully straightening the knee in the early phase
signs: Moderate–large effusion (positive sweep or patellar tap)
Loss of terminal extension and reduced flexion
Increased anterior tibial translation with soft end-feel on Lachman
Antalgic, stiff-knee gait with reduced knee flexion in loading response

subjective: Mechanism: non-contact deceleration, cutting or landing; a contact valgus blow; or hyperextension
Audible 'pop', immediate inability to continue, and swelling within hours (suggests haemarthrosis)
Locking (possible displaced meniscal tear) versus giving way (instability)
Previous knee injuries on either side; family history of ACL injury
Sport, level, position and season timing; work demands; patient goals and preference regarding surgery
Psychological readiness and fear of re-injury
observation: Effusion and loss of quadriceps definition
Gait pattern: reduced knee flexion and quadriceps-avoidance
Inability to fully extend (consider mechanical block)
palpation: Effusion grading with the stroke test
rangeOfMotion: Measure extension including hyperextension relative to the other side
Flexion often limited by effusion early
A springy block to extension suggests a displaced meniscal fragment or a cyclops lesion post-operatively
strength: Quadriceps lag and voluntary activation (straight-leg raise, superior patellar glide)
Isometric or isokinetic quadriceps and hamstring limb symmetry index (LSI) once the knee is calm
Hip abductor and external rotator strength
functional: Single-leg squat and step-down quality (dynamic valgus)
Hop test battery (single, triple, crossover, 6 m timed) once criteria are met
Drop vertical jump or landing assessment for movement quality

specialTests.name: Lachman test
specialTests.purpose: Anterior tibial translation at 20–30° knee flexion
specialTests.procedure: Patient supine, knee in 20–30° flexion. Stabilise the femur with one hand and translate the proximal tibia anteriorly with the other.
specialTests.positive: Increased anterior translation compared with the other side and/or a soft or absent end-point.

specialTests.name: Pivot shift test
specialTests.procedure: From knee extension, apply valgus and internal rotation to the tibia while flexing the knee.
specialTests.positive: The subluxed lateral tibial plateau reduces with a clunk at about 20–40° of flexion.

specialTests.name: Anterior drawer test
specialTests.procedure: Patient supine with knee flexed to 90° and foot stabilised. Draw the tibia anteriorly.
specialTests.positive: Increased anterior translation compared with the other side.

specialTests.name: Lever sign (Lelli test)
specialTests.purpose: ACL integrity when guarding limits other tests
specialTests.procedure: Patient supine. Place a fist under the proximal calf and press down on the distal quadriceps.
specialTests.positive: The heel fails to rise off the couch (the tibia is not lifted by an intact ACL).

clinicalRules.name: Ottawa knee rules
clinicalRules.description: Use to decide on radiographs to exclude fracture in acute knee trauma, e.g. a Segond avulsion fracture or tibial spine avulsion in adolescents.

outcomeMeasures.name: KOOS (Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score)
outcomeMeasures.use: Pain, symptoms, ADL, sport and quality of life; primary outcome in the KANON trial [r10]

outcomeMeasures.name: IKDC Subjective Knee Form
outcomeMeasures.use: Knee-specific function across the rehab course

outcomeMeasures.name: ACL-RSI (Return to Sport after Injury) scale
outcomeMeasures.use: Psychological readiness to return to sport [r16]

outcomeMeasures.name: Tegner activity scale
outcomeMeasures.use: Activity level before and after injury

imaging.indication: When the Ottawa knee rules are positive or a fracture is suspected
imaging.findings: Segond fracture (lateral capsular avulsion, highly specific for ACL rupture); tibial spine avulsion in adolescents

imaging.indication: Confirm the diagnosis and stage associated injuries to guide management
imaging.findings: Discontinuous ACL fibres; lateral compartment bone bruises; meniscal tears including ramp lesions; chondral injury; MCL/PLC injury

differentials.name: Lateral patellar dislocation
differentials.distinguishing: Also causes a pivot-and-haemarthrosis presentation. Look for medial patellar tenderness (MPFL), a positive apprehension test and an intact Lachman.

differentials.name: Meniscal tear
differentials.distinguishing: Twisting injury with joint-line tenderness and locking or catching. Swelling is often delayed over 24 h, and Lachman is negative if isolated.

differentials.name: MCL sprain
differentials.distinguishing: Valgus mechanism with medial pain and tenderness. Valgus stress laxity at 30°. Usually little effusion if isolated.

differentials.name: PCL injury
differentials.distinguishing: Dashboard or fall on a flexed knee. Posterior sag and a positive posterior drawer. A false-positive anterior drawer can occur from the sagged position.

differentials.name: Tibial plateau fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Higher-energy or older patient, unable to weight-bear, positive Ottawa rules. Lipohaemarthrosis on imaging.

differentials.name: Posterolateral corner injury
differentials.distinguishing: Varus or hyperextension mechanism. Dial test positive and varus laxity at 30°. Often combined with a cruciate injury.

redFlags: Absent or reduced distal pulses, a cold foot or a gross deformity: suspect knee dislocation with popliteal artery injury. Refer to emergency immediately.
A knee locked in flexion that cannot be extended: suspect a displaced bucket-handle meniscal tear. Arrange urgent orthopaedic review.
Inability to perform a straight-leg raise against gravity with a palpable gap: suspect extensor mechanism rupture.
Bony tenderness or inability to weight-bear 4 steps (Ottawa knee rules): arrange radiographs.
After surgery, calf pain, swelling or breathlessness (DVT/PE), or fever with a hot, increasingly painful knee (septic arthritis): arrange urgent medical review.

management.principles: Use shared decision-making between two evidence-based pathways [r11]. The first is rehabilitation first, with optional delayed reconstruction if functional instability persists. The second is early reconstruction followed by rehabilitation, ideally after a pre-operative phase that restores a quiet knee, full extension and quadriceps control. In young active adults, rehab-first and early reconstruction gave similar KOOS outcomes at two years, and about 60% of the rehab-first group avoided surgery [r10]. Reconstruction is generally favoured for people who want to return to high-level pivoting sport, who have recurrent giving way despite good rehabilitation, or who have a repairable meniscal tear. Every pathway needs a long, criteria-based rehabilitation program [r12].

medical.name: ACL reconstruction (hamstring, patellar tendon or quadriceps tendon graft)
medical.description: Arthroscopic replacement of the ACL with an autograft (or allograft). Indicated for persistent functional instability, high-level pivoting sport, or repairable meniscal injury. Early surgery was not superior to rehab with optional delayed surgery at two years [r10].

medical.name: Analgesia and short-term anti-inflammatory medication
medical.description: Simple analgesia and short NSAID courses to control pain and effusion in the acute phase. They may help limit inflammation-driven AMI [r7].

medical.name: Aspiration of a tense haemarthrosis
medical.description: Performed by a doctor for a very tense, painful effusion that is limiting quadriceps activation. It reduces pain and inhibition.

medical.name: Hinged knee brace
medical.description: Short-term use when a concomitant MCL injury or meniscal repair needs protection, per surgeon protocol. There is no routine benefit for an isolated ACL reconstruction.

physio.name: Structured, criteria-based progressive exercise therapy
physio.description: Combined strength and neuromuscular training progressed by objective criteria rather than time, continued for 9–12 months after reconstruction or as first-line treatment [r11,r12].

physio.name: Pre-operative rehabilitation (prehabilitation)
physio.description: Restore full extension, resolve effusion and build quadriceps strength and normal gait before surgery. Pre-operative function predicts post-operative outcome [r12].

physio.name: Open and closed kinetic chain quadriceps strengthening
physio.description: Closed-chain from day 1. Open-chain knee extension from about 4 weeks after reconstruction in a restricted range (90–45°), progressing to full range and heavy loading later [r12].

physio.name: Neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) and strategies for AMI
physio.description: Use NMES alongside exercise. Cryotherapy and effusion control may help disinhibit the quadriceps early [r7,r12].

physio.name: Cryotherapy
physio.description: Short-term relief of post-operative pain. It has limited effect on long-term outcomes [r12].

physio.name: Neuromuscular injury-prevention training (secondary prevention)
physio.description: Landing, cutting, balance and strength programs integrated into training before and after RTS. They roughly halve ACL injury risk [r20].

physio.name: Psychological readiness and education
physio.description: Screen with the ACL-RSI and address fear of re-injury with graded exposure and goal setting. Frame RTS as a continuum [r15,r16].

education: The ACL does not heal back together, but many people regain a stable, functional knee with good rehabilitation, with or without surgery.
Surgery is a choice, not an emergency. Both pathways can lead to good outcomes; the decision depends on your sport, your goals and whether your knee keeps giving way.
Rehab after reconstruction takes at least 9 months. Returning earlier or before passing tests greatly increases the risk of another injury.
Getting the knee fully straight and the quadriceps working in the first weeks is the most important early job.
Long-term knee health depends on strength, staying active, healthy body weight and avoiding re-injury.

rehab.overview: Progression is criteria-based, following the KNGF guideline phases: a pre-operative or acute phase, then impairment-based, sport-specific and return-to-play phases [r12]. Each stage below gives typical post-reconstruction timeframes. For the rehab-first pathway use the same criteria, usually progressing faster through stages 1–2. A graft donor site, meniscal repair or concurrent ligament surgery may add restrictions. Always confirm the surgeon's protocol.

stages.name: Calm the knee & restore extension
goals: Full passive extension equal to the other side
Active quadriceps contraction with no lag
Normal gait with or without crutches
precautions: Avoid prolonged pillow under the knee (flexion contracture)
Monitor for DVT and infection after surgery

exercises.name: Quadriceps sets with towel under heel
exercises.cues: Push the back of the knee down and lift the heel slightly

exercises.name: Heel slides
exercises.cues: Slide slowly into flexion within comfort; return to full extension

exercises.name: Straight-leg raise
exercises.cues: Lock the knee straight first, then lift

exercises.name: Prone hangs / extension stretch
exercises.dosage: 3 × 2–5 min daily if extension is lacking

progressionCriteria: Effusion grade ≤ trace on stroke test

stages.name: Strength & neuromuscular control
precautions: Open-chain knee extension from week 4 in 90–45° only after a hamstring graft; progress range by week 12 per protocol [r12]
Increase load no faster than effusion allows (soreness rules)

exercises.name: Squat (to box, progressing depth and load)
exercises.cues: Knees over toes, weight through the whole foot

exercises.name: Seated knee extension (restricted range)
exercises.cues: Move from 90° to 45° and stop; progress range over time

exercises.name: Step-ups and step-downs
exercises.cues: Keep the pelvis level and the knee tracking over the second toe

exercises.name: Romanian deadlift / hamstring bridge
exercises.cues: Hinge at the hips with a long spine

progressionCriteria: Single-leg squat to 60° without valgus collapse

stages.name: Power, running & landing

exercises.name: Split squat and Bulgarian split squat (heavy)
Jump-squat and drop landing drills
exercises.cues: Land quietly with hips and knees bent

progressionCriteria: Good landing mechanics on video analysis

stages.name: Return to sport & performance
goals: Sport-specific change of direction and reactive agility
Graded return to training then competition
precautions: No return to competitive pivoting sport before 9 months post-reconstruction [r14]
Monitor workload as training volume increases

exercises.name: Planned then unplanned cutting drills
exercises.cues: Lower the centre of mass and keep the knee over the foot

exercises.name: Reactive agility and decision-making drills
exercises.cues: Respond to a ball or opponent cue

exercises.name: Heavy strength maintenance (squat, split squat, hamstrings)

progressionCriteria: Patient-reported knee function > 90% (e.g. KOS-ADL, global rating) [r14]
Completion of full, unrestricted team training

criteria: Hop test battery (single, triple, crossover, 6 m timed) ≥ 90% symmetry [r14]
Good movement quality during landing and cutting [r12]
Psychological readiness (e.g. ACL-RSI) and a shared decision with the athlete, coach and surgeon [r15,r16]
tests: Isokinetic or hand-held dynamometry quadriceps/hamstring LSI
Single, triple, crossover and 6 m timed hop tests
Drop vertical jump / landing error scoring

prognosis: After reconstruction, 81% of people return to some sport, but only 65% return to their pre-injury level and 55% return to competitive sport [r17]. Second ACL injuries (graft or contralateral) occur in about 15% overall and in about 23% of athletes under 25 who return to sport. Most of these occur early after return [r18]. Meeting objective RTS criteria and delaying return until 9 months both markedly reduce re-injury: re-injury occurred in 38.2% of those who failed the criteria versus 5.6% of those who passed [r14]. About half of people develop knee osteoarthritis within 10–20 years, and surgery does not appear to prevent this [r19].
prevention: Neuromuscular training programs (landing, cutting, balance, strength, plyometrics) reduce all ACL injuries by about 50% and non-contact ACL injuries in females by about 67% [r20].
Coach landing with hip and knee flexion and avoidance of dynamic valgus ('knee over toe') [r3,r4].
Integrate the program into regular warm-ups (≥2–3 times per week) and continue it through the season.
clinicalPearls: A tense effusion within hours of a non-contact pivot or landing is an ACL rupture until proven otherwise. Examine with Lachman early, before guarding sets in.
A negative pivot shift in the clinic does not exclude ACL rupture (sensitivity ~24%) because guarding stops the shift. A positive one almost confirms it [r9].
Treat loss of extension as an emergency of rehab. A few degrees lost early is hard to win back and drives quadriceps weakness and patellofemoral pain.
Quadriceps weakness is the hallmark deficit. Measure it objectively and repeatedly; 'looks strong' is not a test.
Time is not a criterion. Use 9 months as the minimum and objective tests as the gate [r14].
Ask about fear. A low ACL-RSI score is a common, modifiable reason athletes do not return [r16,r17].

animation.title: How a non-contact ACL rupture happens

captions.text: A basketball player decelerates hard to side-step off the right foot.
The foot plants ahead of the body with the knee only about 20° bent.
Within ~40 ms the knee collapses into valgus as the tibia rotates internally.
Quadriceps pull and ground force shear the tibia forward, and the ACL fails.
A 'pop', the knee gives way, and the athlete goes down.
Zooming into the right knee, viewed from the front with the patella reflected.
The ACL runs from the lateral femoral condyle, inside the notch, to the front of the tibial plateau.
Valgus, internal rotation and anterior shear load the ACL beyond its capacity.
Fibres fail in mid-substance: a complete (grade III) rupture with frayed, recoiling ends.
As the tibia subluxes, the femur and tibia impact laterally, causing a 'kissing' bone bruise.
Meniscal and MCL injuries often accompany the rupture.
Torn vessels bleed into the joint, and a tense haemarthrosis develops within hours.
Synovial fluid and a synovial cap over each stump stop the ends bridging, so the ACL does not heal by itself.
Healthy ligament: crimped type I collagen fibres aligned along the line of load.
Under load the crimp straightens and the fibres stretch elastically.
Beyond the elastic range, fibrils slide and begin to fail.
Sequential fibre failure ends in complete rupture.
Torn capillaries bleed. Synovial fluid dilutes the clot, so there is no scaffold to heal on.
Inflammation: neutrophils, then macrophages, clear debris over the first ~3 weeks.
Cells and new vessels proliferate, but a synovial layer caps each stump and no bridge forms.
The stumps retract and remodel. Stability must come from muscle control or a reconstructed graft.
